passages.t: Bildad again: the lamp of the wicked goes out
passages.happening:
‘Then Bildad the Shuhite replied’ (verse 1). “How long until you end these speeches? Show some sense, and then we can talk. Why are we regarded as cattle, as stupid in your sight?” (verses 2-3). Should the earth be abandoned, or the rocks moved, because Job is angry?

“Indeed, the lamp of the wicked is extinguished; the flame of his fire does not glow. The light in his tent grows dark, and the lamp beside him goes out” (verses 5-6). His stride shortens, and his own schemes trip him up. ‘For his own feet lead him into a net, and he wanders into its mesh’ (verse 8). A trap seizes his heel, a snare grips him, a noose lies hidden in the ground.
passages.hearers:
Bildad does not answer Job's hope of a witness in heaven at all. He gives the most concentrated picture of the wicked man's end in the book, and like Eliphaz he offers Job no way back. In chapter 8 he at least promised that God would fill Job's mouth with laughter. Here the promise is gone.

His case, in the form he would sign, is this. The world is not rearranged for one angry man. The moral order is fixed: the wicked are caught in their own schemes, and their lights go out.

The lamp was a small clay oil lamp that burned through the night in many homes. A living family kept its lamp lit, and a lamp going out was a picture of a household dying. The six words for traps in verses 8 to 10 come from hunting and fowling, where nets, spring traps and hidden nooses were set along paths. It is a true insight that sin tends to entangle the one who commits it. The error is to read it backward.
passages.later: Proverbs says the same of the wicked: “The iniquities of a wicked man entrap him; the cords of his sin entangle him” (Proverbs 5:22).
passages.asks: Bildad was offended that Job did not take his counsel. Ask whether you have ever grown angry with someone for not accepting your help. And ask whether the help was what they needed.

passages.t: No tent, no root, no name
passages.happening:
‘Terrors frighten him on every side and harass his every step’ (verse 11). Calamity waits at his side. Disease eats his skin; ‘the firstborn of death devours his limbs’ (verse 13). He is torn from his tent and marched off to the king of terrors.

Fire lives in his tent, and burning sulfur rains on his home. His roots dry up and his branches wither. ‘The memory of him perishes from the earth, and he has no name in the land’ (verse 17). He is driven from light into darkness. ‘He has no offspring or posterity among his people, no survivor where he once lived’ (verse 19). People in the west and the east are horrified.

“Surely such is the dwelling of the wicked and the place of one who does not know God” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The king of terrors is death pictured as a ruler who receives the dead as captives. In texts from Ugarit, Death appears as a god called Mot who swallows his victims, and some interpreters hear that background here. The firstborn of death is probably a fatal disease, death's eldest son doing his father's work. The burning sulfur recalls Sodom and Gomorrah, the Bible's classic picture of sudden judgment.

To die with no name and no children was the deepest fear of the ancient world. A man lived on through his children, who carried his name and kept his memory.

Almost every image matches something that has happened to Job: fire from heaven (1:16), his children dead (1:19), his skin diseased (2:7), his honor gone. Bildad knows all of this. He never names Job, but the portrait is drawn in his likeness, and it cannot be heard as anything but aimed at him.
passages.later: The burning sulfur recalls Sodom: ‘Then the LORD rained down sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah’ (Genesis 19:24).
passages.hard:
Why does Scripture include such a cruel speech to a suffering man?

Bildad describes the very losses of a man whose children have died and whose body is diseased as the marks of one who does not know God. Readers rightly find it cruel. The book includes it because Job is an argument, and it needs the friends' case in its fullest form in order to test it. Bildad is a sincere believer defending what he sees as God's justice, and much of what he says about the wicked is true in general. The problem is that he treats it as a formula that explains every case, and so he condemns an innocent man.

At the end of the book God says the friends have not spoken rightly of him (42:7). Reading Bildad carefully helps readers recognize the same pattern when it appears in their own thinking and speech. Losing a child, or a home, or one's health is never in itself a sign that someone does not know God.

Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Bildad drew the wicked man's portrait from Job's own losses. Ask whether you have ever looked at someone's misfortune and quietly assumed they deserved it. And ask how you would want your own losses to be spoken of.
